[0] everyday_reading (E): Everyday intuition, and some older languages, treat a new or empty quantity as zero ("nothing yet means 0"). A Java local variable has no value at all until it is assigned, and the compiler rejects any read before that.
[1] misconception (M) -> LocalVariablesAutoInitialized: wrong rule: local variables get a default value on their own. Right rule: A local variable has no value until it is assigned, and using it before then does not compile.
[2] inconsistent_trace (T) -> LocalVariablesAutoInitialized: Points to LT (along every control-flow path, an assignment must come before each read). Applied unevenly, a student checks straight-line code but assumes a variable assigned in only one branch of an if, or inside a loop, is assigned afterwards. (here mixing in: "local variables get a default value on their own")

[0] names_the_element (N): Definite assignment: the compile-time rule that a local variable must certainly have been assigned before any read of it.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Every access of a local variable must be preceded by an assignment on every possible path, or the program does not compile. The analysis ignores run-time values, except for constant booleans and the operators && || ?:.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): The compiler walks the control flow. After a declaration with no initializer the variable is unassigned, and an assignment makes it assigned on that path. Where paths merge (after if/else) it counts as assigned only if every incoming path assigned it, and an assignment inside a while body does not count after the loop.
[1] output_prediction (OP): The result appears at compile time: the code either compiles or reports 'variable x might not have been initialized'. No default value is ever produced for a local variable.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): The first assignment (initialization) moves a variable from unassigned to holding a value, and only then may it be read.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): A declaration without an initializer leaves the local unassigned. Writing = value in the declaration satisfies the rule at once.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): A local variable has no value until it is assigned: using it first is a compile-time error. An array element is given a default value (0, 0.0, false) when the array is created with new, so it can be read before any assignment.
[2] purpose_of_the_whole (P): The rule guarantees that no program reads a meaningless value. The matching plan is to initialize counters and accumulators before the loop that updates them (int sum = 0; then sum += i inside the loop).

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> LocalVariablesAutoInitialized: Moving an initialization into one branch of an if, or into a loop body, breaks compilation of the reads that follow. Adding an else branch that also assigns, or initializing at the declaration, restores it.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Initialize at the declaration whenever a sensible first value exists (0 for counters and sums). Leave the declaration bare only when every branch that follows assigns it. The rule covers local variables only: array elements and fields get default values.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A local variable must be definitely assigned before it is read. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: A read reachable on a path with no assignment: declared without initializer, or assigned only inside an if without else, a loop body, or a switch case: 'variable might not have been initialized'.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A blank final variable must be assigned at most once. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Assigning a final local on two paths that can both run, or again inside a loop: 'variable might already have been assigned'.

wrong: int x; inside main starts at 0, so x can be used before anything is assigned to it. | right: A local variable has no value until it is assigned, and using it before then does not compile.

A local variable has no value until it is assigned: using it first is a compile-time error. An array element is given a default value (0, 0.0, false) when the array is created with new, so it can be read before any assignment.
A declared local variable has no defined value until it is assigned, and the compiler rejects any read before that assignment.
